wstep: This card describes mango leather following the NCHFP recipe: mango purée with honey and spices is dried in a dehydrator at 140 °F (60 °C) for about 10 hours.

akapity: NCHFP does not describe aam papad: this card is the NCHFP mango leather recipe, not traditional aam papad; it does not cover papaya.
4 cups mango purée (from about 4 large, unripe mangoes), 1 cup clover honey, 1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon, 1/4 teaspoon ground nutmeg and 1/4 teaspoon ground cloves.
This makes about 2 dryer trays 14 inches (about 36 cm) in diameter, or 8 fruit rolls.
You may omit the honey (unsweetened leather); for a lighter colour add 1/4 teaspoon (750 mg) of ascorbic acid to the purée with the spices.
Do not give leather made with honey to infants under 12 months; for them, leave the honey out.
Preheat the dehydrator to 140 °F (60 °C).
Wash, peel and chop the mangoes and purée until smooth; pass the purée through a food mill or sieve, discard the coarse fibre and mix in the honey and spices thoroughly.
Lightly spray two dehydrator fruit roll liners with vegetable oil cooking spray and spread the purée evenly 1/4 inch (about 6 mm) thick.
Do not use trays or screens made of galvanized mesh; also avoid copper and aluminium mesh.
Dry continuously for about 10 hours with the air temperature held steadily at 140 °F (60 °C); check it periodically with a thermometer.
The leather is ready when there are no sticky areas and touching gently in several places near the centre leaves no indentation; the time depends strongly on the humidity of the room.
An electric dehydrator gives the most reliable results; an oven is suitable only if it can hold 140–145 °F (about 60–63 °C).
Line a cookie sheet with edges with plastic wrap, smoothing out the wrinkles, or spray it with vegetable oil; do not use waxed paper or aluminium foil.
Leave the oven door open 2–6 inches (about 5–15 cm) and keep the air temperature at about 140 °F (60 °C), checking it with a thermometer; if it gets too high, turn the oven off for a while.
Begin checking a large leather at 8–10 hours.
Peel the leather from the liners while still warm; if it cools too much, re-warm it slightly in the dehydrator.
Cut it into quarters, lay it on plastic food wrap 1–2 inches (about 2.5–5 cm) longer at each end and roll it up; when cool, twist the ends of the wrap tightly.
Pack only completely cooled rolls: warm dried food sweats, and that moisture can be enough for mould to grow.
Store the rolls short term, up to about 1 month, in freezer-quality zippered plastic bags or airtight plastic containers, in a cool, dark, dry place.
For storage up to 1 year, keep tightly wrapped rolls in the freezer.
Store the dried fruit in clean, dry canning jars, plastic freezer containers with tight-fitting lids or plastic freezer bags.
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items.
Pack amounts that can be used at one time: each opening exposes the dried fruit to air and moisture, which lowers quality and can lead to spoilage.
Vacuum packaging is not a preservation method by itself: removing oxygen increases the risk of botulism, and a product that needs refrigeration still needs it.
Check the dried fruit often (glass shows condensation); if it has taken up moisture but is not spoiled, use it at once or dry it again and repack it.
Throw away mouldy dried fruit; also throw away dried fruit that smells off.
